## Power Analysis

We based our sample size on a simulation-based power analysis using the  `mixedpower` package in R (@kumle2021). The simulation power analysis was based on pilot data we collected via SONA using the PsychoPy experiment platform (@Pierce2018) and the Pavlovia server (www.pavlovia.org) from November until the end of the Fall semester. The script to run this power analysis is located on our OSF page here: . The results of this analysis suggested we would need to collect 80 participants (40 in each group) to have 80% power to detect a specific effect of prequestions. Given this, our goal was to run 80 participants. It is important to note that this is also twice the sample size @meskinicl2012 ran in there experiment 2, which this study is closely based on.

```{r}
# install mixedpower
if (!require("devtools")) {
    install.packages("devtools", dependencies = TRUE)}
devtools::install_github("DejanDraschkow/mixedpower") # mixedpower is hosted on GitHub

# load library
library(mixedpower)
```
The DV is number of points earned for answering each question. Because we are modeling proportions (points earned on each question/total points) we fit a binomial mixed model to predict proportion correct on polio questions as a function of group type (prequstioned vs. control). We then used this pilot data to calculate power for our main comparison of interest (Prequestion > Control). 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(glmmTMB)
library(gamlss)

scored <- read_csv(here::here("Scored_Data", "pilot_scored_data", "all_scored_jg.csv"))
                   

head(scored)

scored_polio <- scored %>% 
  dplyr::filter(expName!="preQ_TB") %>%
  dplyr::select(Sub.ID, expName, questnum, Condition, earned_points) %>%
  dplyr::filter(Condition=="Polio") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(totalscore=6)


model1 <- glmer(earned_points/totalscore~ expName + (1|Sub.ID)+ (1|questnum),  family="binomial", weights=totalscore, data=scored_polio)

summary(model1)
#report(model1)
emmeans(model1, "expName")

pairs(emmeans(model1, "expName"))

```

```{r}

library(mixedpower)
# ------------------------------------------ #
# RUN SIMULATION
power_FLP <- mixedpower(model = model1, data = scored_polio,
                        fixed_effects = c("expName"), 
                        simvar = "Sub.ID", steps = c(50,60,70,80,100),
                        critical_value = 2, n_sim = 1000)
```
```{r}
# ------------------------------------------ #
# PLOT RESULTS
multiplotPower(power_FLP)
```
## Materials

The experimental text was a 690 word, multi-topic text about Polio and TB taken from @meskinicl2012 that discussed the Gates Foundation’s role in eradicating disease in the developing world (see this link for the text: ). The text consisted of 39 sentences, and was presented over five computer screens ranging in length from 8 to 11 lines. Sentence topics were divided into two categories (Polio TB sentences). Polio sentences were the sentences from the reading that centered on polio topics. To come up with our polio prequestions, we choose 5 releavant sentences from the text and derived 5 prequestions from information conatined in those sentecnes.  we used the exact same procedure to come up with TB questions. Questions could be percentage-based, yes/no, or multi-part. The total number of points participants could receive is 12 points. 

## Procedure

At the start of the experiment, participants will be randomly assigned to one of two instructional conditions (Prequestion or  Control). After completing an informed consent process the participant will be either be given prequestions related to Polio (presented on a separate computer screen), or if in the control group, will be position in the desk-mounted EyeLink 1000 (). both groupsof participants received the following instructions on the computer display:

“The following text contains information about the role the Gates Foundation is playing in the eradication of disease.” In the Question condition, the instructions continued: “Please read it in order to answer the following questions,” followed by four targeted questions (see the materials at this OSF link: ). 

In the Control condition, the instructions concluded, “Please read it carefully.” After the participants had read the prereading instructions, they pressed the space bar on the keyboard in front of them and began to read the experimental text. The experimental text was a 690 word, multi-topic text about Polio and TB taken from @meskinicl2012 The dsicusedd the Gates Foundation’s role in eradicating disease in the developing world. The text consisted of 39 sentences, and was presented over five computer screens ranging in length from 8 to 11 lines. Sentence topics were divided into two categories (Polio and TB). TB sentences were the sentences from the reading that centered on Polio topics. TB sentences consisted of
sentences that covered TB and did not mention polio.

After reading the short text, participants completed a disctor task known as the president recognition task (@Roediger and ??). After completing the president's recognition task, participants completed a 10 question test. In the prequestion group, they were presented with the same 5 questions at the beginning, and 5 non-prequestioned questions that centered on TB. In the control group, there were presented with 10 questions (5 polio questions and 5 TB questions). They were presented with the The first response field was preceded with the following instructions: “Can you remember any additional information about Polio from the passage? If so,please type it below.” The second set of instructions replaced “Polio” with “the Gates Foundation,” and the third replaced “Polio” with “Tuberculosis.” We used a secondary cued recall to elicit any information that participants may not have produced on the original free recall without overly constraining their responses
by posing predetermined questions.
